narrative:
The model determined that you have a 96% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three aspects of your academic record. Your class ranking in your third year of law school was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Standing in the bottom decile, far below the average of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaled to the model that you would likely struggle with the exam. Your LSAT score was the second most important influence; at 25, it sits well below the 37-point average of students who were admitted, further increasing the predicted risk of failure. Your first-year class ranking came third. Like your third-year rank, being in the lowest decile—compared to an average around the sixth decile for accepted applicants—reinforced the same concern about long-term academic performance.

All three features worked in the same direction, each pulling the prediction strongly toward failure rather than success. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.7 (versus 3.23 for accepted students), middle family income, and plan to attend full-time played smaller roles and did not change the overall outlook.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic performance and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score. Targeted bar exam preparation courses or additional practical legal experience could also help demonstrate readiness for the next application cycle.
